name: Oxweld ChemBarrier Overcoat
description:
A long, stiff-shouldered overcoat in industrial yellow-tan, manufactured specifically for Shelf residents and Tier 2 workers who live near chemical processing zones, waste corridors, or the old industrial lakefront. The outer shell is a laminated multi-layer barrier fabric rated for splash resistance against a documented list of common corridor contaminants — sulfuric compounds, petrochemical residue, certain industrial solvents. It is not a full hazmat suit. It is what people wear when they cannot afford a full hazmat suit but still need to walk home through a place that smells wrong. The coat reaches the ankles, has sealed cuffs that can be cinched over gloves, and a high collar with a filtration-compatible face seal along the upper edge.

Oxweld is a Tier 1 to 2 corponation subsidiary — technically a safety equipment manufacturer, not a fashion brand — and their overcoats are sold in bulk through company stores, Shelf distribution points, and licensed resellers near industrial zones. They are ugly. They are effective within their rating. The lining is a rough cotton-poly that chafes in cold weather and the seams are utilitarian at best. But when the eastern wind comes off the old industrial channel and the air tastes metallic, you want one of these between you and whatever is in that air.
functionality: Chemical splash resistance rated for common corridor industrial contaminants. Sealed cuff system. Upper collar designed to interface with standard filtration masks.
what_it_says: You live somewhere the air isn't safe, and you've accepted that as a condition of existence.
story_hooks: A child's version of this coat, small enough for a six-year-old, found abandoned in a Shelf transit hub — inside the collar, a name written in marker and a Tier 3 transit token

A batch of Oxweld overcoats has been circulating that fails its chemical resistance rating at the seams — the failure is recent, the cause is unclear, and people who've been trusting their lives to these coats are only now finding out

An activist group has started customizing these coats with dye and embroidery — turning the industrial ugliness into something defiant — and the imagery is spreading faster than Oxweld's legal team can respond

physical_description.visual_profile: A long, deliberately austere overcoat with rigid shoulders and an almost military bearing. The silhouette is boxy and utilitarian, designed for function over form. Reaches ankle-length with a high, structured collar that reads as protective rather than fashionable. Visual impression is industrial-practical: something you wear because the air outside is unsafe.
physical_description.fit: Oversized and intentionally loose through the torso to accommodate layering and movement. Shoulders are reinforced and squared-off. Sleeves are straight and generous, ending with sealed cuffs that cinch down. The overall cut prioritizes coverage and barrier integrity over body-conforming silhouette.
physical_description.primary_material: Laminated multi-layer barrier fabric — a synthweave composite rated for splash resistance. The outer shell has a slight sheen and stiffness characteristic of industrial laminates. Rough cotton-poly blend lining that is deliberately cheap and utilitarian.
physical_description.texture: Smooth, slightly waxy outer surface with micro-texture designed for easy decontamination wiping. The lamination creates subtle visual stratification. Lining is coarse and prone to pilling. All seams are flat-stitched and visibly utilitarian.
physical_description.color_scheme: Industrial yellow-tan (safety-rated visibility color), sometimes with reflective striping on seams or collar edge. No decorative patterning; any variations are material-based or wear-induced.
physical_description.closures: Full-length heavy-duty zipper with pull-tab rated for industrial use. Reinforced snaps at collar for face-seal compatibility. Cuff cinches use friction-fit or simple friction closures — nothing that might catch on contaminated material.
distinctive_features: High collar with filtration-compatible face seal ridge along upper edge
Sealed cuffs that cinch over gloves
Flat utilitarian seams designed for easy decontamination
Ankle-length cut for full leg coverage
Reinforced shoulder panels with visible stitching
Heavy-duty industrial zipper with oversized pull-tab
Oxweld Safety Systems branding typically stamped or sewn into lining
Slight chemical-resistant sheen on outer surface
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 1–2 boundary. Manufactured by a corpo subsidiary, distributed through official channels and company stores, but affordable enough for Shelf residents. Signals economic precarity at the edge of corpo safety infrastructure.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by industrial workers, chemical corridor residents, waste management staff, and anyone living downwind of processing zones who cannot afford full hazmat protection. Signals: living in a contaminated zone, employed in industrial labor, close to the economic bottom of corpo-adjacent work, acceptance of environmental hazard as lifestyle cost.
physical_description.condition_typical: Usually broken-in and slightly stained from actual use. The outer surface may show faint discoloration from repeated decontamination wiping. Lining is often chafed and pilled. Seams may show stress from repeated cinching. Worn overcoats have a tired, weathered appearance but remain functionally intact.
